1:
The heading and the date come first. Charles Ellicott notes that the superscription unites in an exceptional form the two ideas of prophet and seer, since what follows is a word that Isaiah has seen; Matthew Henry takes the same point devotionally, that he had as full an assurance of its truth as if he had seen it with his bodily eyes. On the date two voices reason from the same fact to different answers. Adam Clarke observes that the seventh verse points to a time when riches abounded and luxury prevailed, and that plenty of silver and gold could only arise from commerce, particularly that of the Red Sea, which confines the prophecy to the period while the port of Elath was in their hands—lost under Ahaz and never recovered—so he places it under Jotham or Uzziah. Ellicott uses the same argument to fix it in the early years of Ahaz, with hardly the shadow of uncertainty: the king described in the next chapter answers to Ahaz, the Philistine influence connects with their invasion in that reign, and the ships of Tarshish belong to a time before Elath was taken.

That the three verses following stand almost word for word in another prophet raises a second question. Clarke supposes the later prophet took them from here, since he did not begin to prophesy until Jotham’s time and this seems one of Isaiah’s earliest. Ellicott is more cautious: whether Isaiah borrowed, or the other borrowed from him, or both drew on an earlier prophet, or each received an identical revelation, is a problem for which we have no adequate data, though he thinks a common older source likeliest. Keil and Delitzsch notice something else unparalleled—no other prophecy begins with the word and, and no other prophetic address, running as this does through exhortation, reproof, threatening and promise, begins with the promise.

John Calvin explains why a vision was given at all. When we are as it were in the midst of destruction, bare promises hardly suffice to support us; so the Lord added this vision by way of confirmation, from which we learn that visions given to the prophets are to be joined to the promises as seals of them—not satisfied with his bare word, God places the events before our eyes. Terror was to be proclaimed until the temple was burnt, and such severity had to be mitigated for believers by some hope; and through the storms in which the Church was nearly overwhelmed, every believer, when shipwrecked, seized this word as a plank by which he might be floated into the harbour.

On the last days the voices agree. John Gill and Clarke cite the rule that wherever the latter days are named the days of the Messiah are meant; Ellicott renders it the after days, the Hebrew conveying remoteness rather than finality; Calvin says the fullness of days began at Christ’s coming but flows on until he appears the second time. Henry adds that gospel times are the last days, since we are to look for no dispensation of grace beyond the gospel and now await a second coming as the older saints awaited the first. On the exalting of the mountain, Ellicott sees a transfigured Jerusalem whose physical elevation answers to its spiritual; Calvin faces the improbability head on, that Zion was a little hill, a handful of earth beside huge mountains, and one whose destruction had just been foretold. Henry keeps to the figure—it shall be so fixed that the gates of hell cannot prevail unless they could pluck up mountains by the roots, and shall not only overcome all opposition but overtop all competition. John Wesley insists the temple meant is not the material one on Moriah but mystically the church, as appears from the flowing of all nations to it, never fulfilled till that temple was destroyed.
3:
The pilgrims are described by what moves them. Keil and Delitzsch call the verse their signal for starting and their song by the way, and say what urges them on is the desire for salvation, which shows itself in the very names they give—the mountain of Jehovah, the house of the God of Jacob. Charles Ellicott says what was precious to the prophet’s heart was that these pilgrims would not come with a formal worship like that rebuked in the previous chapter, but as seekers after truth desiring to be taught. John Calvin presses the word many as an implied contrast, that there will no longer be one nation only devoted to the worship of the true God; and though no whole nation literally journeyed into Judea, yet since the gospel went out from Zion he justly says they come who have with one consent embraced the covenant. He draws two lessons from the invitation. The godly are filled with so ardent a desire to spread religion that no one is satisfied with his own knowledge but wishes to draw others with him, and those who teach should not sit down and command but walk with others as companions—some are severe instructors who urge others forward and yet do not move a step, whereas these believers do not say go up, but lead the way themselves.

The judging that follows is read as arbitration. Keil and Delitzsch put it that, since the nations betake themselves as pupils to the God of revelation, he becomes supreme judge and umpire, so that a dispute is no longer settled by the compulsory force of war but by the word of God, to which all bow with willing submission—and where the word has that power there is no more need of weapons of iron. Ellicott renders the second verb decide or arbitrate and finds a partial fulfilment already, so far as the teaching of Christ has influenced international law; he notes too that the famous image inverts an earlier prophet’s picture of a time of war, which Isaiah must have known, and that he nevertheless proclaims peace as the goal towards which the divine government tends. Calvin sets the doctrine in the place of a king’s sceptre and explains why judgment comes first: through the obstinacy of our nature we make no progress in God’s word until we are subdued, so God takes the office of a judge who by condemning our vices reforms our morals, little being effected by the gospel except where that power leads men to repentance. On the peace itself he is unsentimental: nothing is more desirable, yet while all imagine they desire it every one disturbs it by the madness of his own lusts. Clarke lets the verse become an outcry: what a reproach to humanity is the trade of war, in which men are regularly instructed as in any of the necessary arts.

The exhortation that closes the section turns on the contrast. Keil and Delitzsch say Isaiah presents his contemporaries with this older prophecy of their calling and holds it up as a mirror. Calvin makes the rebuke sharp: nothing could be stranger than that the household should revolt while strangers were drawing near, and he presses it in questions—shall the Gentiles submit to God, and shall you refuse his authority; has so great a light been kindled in every part of the world, and shall you not be enlightened by it? The light, he says, is placed before their feet, and they disregard it by shutting their eyes. John Gill reports the reading that makes these the words of the converted Gentiles to the Jews; Wesley warns against rejecting a light so clear that even the blind Gentiles will discern it; and Ellicott states the condition plainly: the people must learn repentance and walk in the light before they can be light-bearers to other nations.
6:
The first question is who is addressed. Keil and Delitzsch insist the words are addressed to God and not to the people, and dispose of the rendering thou hast given up thy nationality on the ground that the word means people, not nationality—a rendering that would never have been thought of but for the strangeness of so sudden an address to God, though elsewhere the prophecy does become a prayer. John Calvin reads the turn dramatically: the prophet does not charge them in direct terms but, as if bursting into astonishment, breaks off and turns to God—why should I waste words on a nation grown desperate, which thou hast justly rejected? Out of that he draws a consolation for teachers: when we think we are speaking to the deaf we grow faint and are tempted to give over, saying, what am I about, I am beating the air; yet the prophet does not cease to exhort those in whom he saw no ground of hope, and however obstinate the ungodly, we must summon them to the judgment-seat of God, that they be left without excuse. Matthew Henry weighs the sentence: miserable is the condition of a people whom God has forsaken, and great must the provocation be if he forsakes those who have been his own—yet God never leaves any till they first leave him.

The charges are set out most fully by Charles Ellicott. The east from which they were replenished is Syria and Mesopotamia, whose worship Ahaz adopted; the word rendered soothsayers means cloud-diviners, pointing to the claim of raising storms, in all ages a boast of sorcerers, and the conquests of Uzziah had brought Judah into contact with the Philistines, whose oracles drew the people until there was a mania for divination; and the last clause means that they strike hands with the children of strangers, so that the commerce expanded under Uzziah opened the way to a foreign impurity of worship and life, and the sense of being a separate people wore away. Henry says the same, that God had set them apart as a peculiar people and they naturalised foreigners; John Wesley that they delighted in such company, making leagues and marriages. Adam Clarke works on the words: several copies read that they have joined themselves to the children of strangers, in marriage or worship; on the divination clause he judges the sentence imperfect, conjecturing that two similar words stood together, one dropping out, so that the sense was divination from the east.

The wealth of the next verse is measured against a law. Clarke sets it against the command that the king should not multiply horses, nor greatly multiply silver and gold, and observes that Uzziah followed Solomon’s example, recovering the port of Elath and with it the commerce that had once made silver as plenteous as stones; that law, he adds, was a standing trial whether prince and people trusted God their deliverer. Keil and Delitzsch put it more bluntly: the glory of Solomon, revived under Uzziah and sustained through Jotham, carried the curse of the law with it, since standing armies and stores of treasure minister to carnal self-reliance. Ellicott adds that Isaiah treats the chariots, with the other prophet, as the beginning of sin, since for him the true King was to come not with chariots and horses but riding as the judges of Israel had ridden. Calvin marks the order of the indictment—idolatry, then covetousness, then a sinful confidence—and is careful about the second: it was not in itself to be condemned that the nation had abundance, but that they burned with insatiable covetousness and trusted in it, there being no end of their treasures because their eagerness goes beyond the bounds of nature. John Gill, judging the description fits no period of the nation’s history, applies the passage instead to a later ecclesiastical power and its revenues.
8:
The word chosen for the idols carries the argument. Charles Ellicott notes that it means vain or false gods and seems deliberately contrasted with the ordinary word for gods, so that it may fairly be rendered no-gods; the worship was conspicuous from the first under Ahaz, though prominent already under Jotham. John Calvin presses the same point: the Spirit intended by that word to reprove the madness of men who imagined that by relying on such inventions they came nearer to God, and against those who plead that images are the books of the unlearned he answers that the unlearned, led away by gross fancies, imagine to themselves earthly and carnal gods—so that another prophet calls idols not merely useless but teachers of lies. On the making he is blunter still: it is shocking that as soon as a block of wood which had lain neglected receives the finishing stroke from a mortal man, he worships it as though it had been made a god, honouring his own workmanship with a title he cannot bestow on himself. He adds how quickly the thing spreads—where idols are set up among us we scarcely ever fail to abuse them, for it is like fire applied to a pile of wood, and wood is not readier to catch than we are to follow superstition.

Adam Clarke enters a qualification the others do not. Both Uzziah and Jotham are said to have done what was right, that is, to have maintained the legal worship against idolatry, save that the high places were not removed; and worshipping at high places does not necessarily imply idolatry. We may presume, then, that public idolatrous worship was not permitted in their time, so that the idols named here must have been meant for private and secret use—probably the household images so often mentioned, kept for divination and consulted as oracles. John Gill, consistent with his reading of the chapter, applies the verse to images set up in the churches and houses of a later communion. Keil and Delitzsch draw the structural conclusion: this was a state ripe for judgment, from which the prophet could proceed at once to the proclamation of judgment itself.

The last verse is read either as the sin or its punishment. Ellicott sets out the choice: the received version applies the bowing and humbling to the prostrations of idol-worshippers of low and high degree, while others refer them to the punishment of that idolatry, so that the mean man must be bowed down and the great man humbled. Clarke takes the second and makes the correspondence exact: they bowed down to their idols, therefore they shall be bowed down under the avenging hand of God. Calvin reports both and prefers the second as agreeing best with the scope of the passage, hearing an allusion in the very words: they have bowed down before idols, therefore God will bow them down under a vast weight of calamities. Keil and Delitzsch describe its sweep: small and great alike, men lost in the crowd and men who rose above it, were to be thrown down from their false eminence, the judgment following by inward necessity from the worldly and ungodly glory of things as they stood. On the closing clause the voices divide again. Ellicott records that as a prayer it has parallels, but thinks the rendering and thou canst not forgive them preferable, the sin being treated as one unto death for which it is vain to pray; Clarke likewise prefers and thou wilt not forgive them. Calvin holds that the two come to the same thing, since when the prophets pour out such prayers under the dictation of the Spirit they are threatening just punishment—and he adds the qualification the passage needs, that a remnant is tacitly reserved, what is spoken of being not every individual but the body of the people.
10:
The command to hide makes the judgment vivid. John Calvin says that because ungodly men lull themselves in indifference about God’s threatenings, the prophets, to produce terror, add lively descriptions that bring the matter under men’s eyes; God’s judgment is more to be dreaded than a thousand deaths, so that to escape it a man might wish to go down into the grave. On the clause about majesty he adds that it is according to the measure of his own glory that God is to be dreaded by the ungodly, in whose destruction he displays his boundless power; and punishment does not reform them, who are merely forced to tremble, whereas the elect, subdued by strokes, learn to bear the yoke. From this he draws a rule for preachers: drowsy consciences must be awakened by the judgment of God, for though we often sing to the deaf, terror pierces even hearts of iron, and some are healed. Matthew Henry turns the verse into observations—that those who will not fear God and flee to him will be forced to fear him and flee from him to a refuge of lies; and that it is vain to seek refuge in the caves of the earth when the earth itself is shaken, since there is then no shelter but in God and things above. Charles Ellicott supplies the background: the limestone caverns of the country were natural asylums in times of terror, and here we may trace the impression left by the earthquake under Uzziah, so that the prophet foresees a like panic. John Wesley puts it simply: such calamities are coming that they will be ready to hide in rocks and caves.

Adam Clarke makes a textual addition. On the authority of the Greek, supported by another version and a manuscript, he inserts a line that stands twice later in the chapter—when he ariseth to strike the earth with terror—judging it omitted here by mistake, though another collation supplies no manuscript in its favour. At the next verse he reports a proposed repointing which would rectify the construction but which no manuscript or version confirms.

The humbling of the lofty begins the chapter’s refrain. Ellicott renders the clauses of the mean man and the great man, since the self-assertion which is the essence of pride is found at both extremes of social life; and he notes that the verb for the Lord being exalted carries the image of a rock-citadel offering the one safe asylum in danger—setting the true refuge against the rocks men crawl into. Henry describes the fall: the eyes that aim high and the countenance in which the pride of the heart shows itself shall be cast down in shame, and the things men were proud of they shall be ashamed of. Pride, he says, will one way or another have a fall, brought down either by grace convincing men of its evil or by providence depriving them of what they were proud of—so that he who exalts himself shall be abased, abasing himself in true repentance or else abased by God. Calvin explains why the pride grew: where crimes pass unpunished it is a sort of cloud held before our eyes which hinders us from beholding the glory of the Lord, whereas when he takes vengeance that glory shines out—which is why, as another writer observed, because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, the heart of men is fully set to do evil. Keil and Delitzsch take up the phrase that day: the Lord has a day, one already existing as a finished divine thought in the wisdom by which history is guided, whose secret he revealed to the prophets, who proclaimed it from early times with one uniform watchword. John Gill, keeping his own application, reads the lofty looks of the power that exalts itself above all that is called God.
12:
The day is defined before its objects. Charles Ellicott renders the opening literally, that the Lord of hosts has a day, and notes that in the prophets any time of special judgment or mercy is a day of Jehovah, the phrase being prominent already in Isaiah’s forerunner. He finds the repeated lifted up significant, as showing that the prophet saw in self-assertion the root evil of his time; and he sets beside it the way the devout historian of Greece read the history he told, seeing the loftiest trees most exposed to the lightning-flash and the loftiest monarch most liable to a divine Nemesis. John Calvin infers from the heaping up of words how bold the wickedness of that time was, and says we need not wonder the prophet labours so hard, considering how difficult it is to bend men who, relying on their wealth, are afraid of nothing and suppose their rank exists so that whatever they do shall pass unpunished. The charge is not confined to the great: persons of the lowest rank swell with pride too, for as the proverb runs, every man carries within him the heart of a king, and even the basest, if you do but prick them, vomit out the poison of an intolerable arrogance. On the particle before the divine name he holds that it keeps its force, since the prophet appoints a fixed day as in a judicial trial—and draws from it that God avows himself the enemy of all the proud. John Gill calls it the day peculiarly his, fixed and appointed; John Wesley, the time of God’s vengeance upon sinners.

Whether the trees and hills are literal is the question of the next verse. Keil and Delitzsch describe the arrangement first, that the prophet enumerates the high things two and two, so that the day comes upon everything lofty in nature; then they raise the doubt—wherefore upon all this majestic beauty, and is it merely figurative? They report the view that it describes the grand buildings of the time of Uzziah and Jotham, for which timber was fetched from Lebanon and from the slopes of Bashan, and resist the notion that trees can stand for the houses built out of them. Adam Clarke supplies the fullest defence of the figurative reading. These verses, he says, are a striking example of that way of writing which characterises the parabolical style, exhibiting things divine, moral and political by images drawn from nature and art; and Hebrew poetry is more regular in this than any other, having images appropriated to particular subjects—cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan for kings and potentates, high mountains and lofty hills for kingdoms and states and cities, and ships of Tarshish with the art employed in adorning them for merchants and men enriched by commerce. He adds that ships of Tarshish stand by a figure for ships in general, especially those trading between distant countries.

Calvin agrees that the allegory sheds light rather than obscuring: however high a mortal’s wishes may reach, he will never attain the height of the cedars, and it is as easy for God to throw those down as for a breath of wind to scatter fallen leaves. He guards against the wrong inference—God is not actually angry with the mountains and trees, but in the harmless creatures the prophet holds out the judgment of God, to convince unprincipled men that their presumption will not pass unpunished. Ellicott lets the two senses stand together: the cedars and the oaks, and those who were as the cedars and oaks in their pride, should all alike be shattered. Wesley takes both at once, the trees thrown down by winds or earthquakes or torn by lightning, and the stately houses built of cedar and oak destroyed with them; while Gill keeps to persons, reading the cedars of the kings of the earth.
14:
The list moves from nature to what men have built. Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition: the glory of nature is followed by what is lofty in the world of men—magnificent fortifications, grand commercial buildings, and treasures that minister to the lust of the eye. They give the fortifications a history, since it was by erecting works both lofty and steep that Uzziah and Jotham endeavoured to serve Jerusalem, the chronicler recording that Uzziah built strong towers over the weakest points of the city and towers in the desert as well, to secure the country and its flocks. Charles Ellicott agrees that, generic as the words are, they refer especially to the fortifications which were the glory of Uzziah’s reign; on the mountains he suggests the prophet may have had in mind the psalm in which the Lord breaks the cedars of Lebanon, and that the words must literally have found fulfilment in the ravages of the Assyrian armies. John Wesley notes only that the hills were what men used to betake themselves to in times of danger.

John Calvin insists that here the language is not figurative. Men who think themselves well defended congratulate themselves that they no longer need God’s assistance; under the name of towers the prophet names the object of a false confidence, for wherever a place seems impregnable there do irreligious men build their nest, that they may look down from it upon heaven and earth, imagining themselves beyond all the uncertainties of fortune. And although such things are not in themselves evil, yet because they take too large a share of our attention it is with great propriety that the prophet sharpens his pen against them.

The ships and the treasures draw out the fullest comment. Ellicott takes the phrase to point to the commerce of the Red Sea carried on by the fleets of Uzziah and Jotham, and perhaps to the Mediterranean trade as well, the name having come to serve generically for all ships of that class, whether crossing to Spain, circumnavigating Africa, or passing to Ophir. The clause about pleasant pictures he renders all imagery of delight, and infers from its standing beside the ships that it takes in the works of art they brought from East and West, for which there was a mania among the higher classes in Jerusalem like that which later fastened upon china, or pictures, or carvings in ivory; he instances the ivory beds and the pillars of marble on sockets of fine gold, and observes that the aestheticism of the Roman Empire, of the Renaissance, and of our own time presents obvious parallels. John Wesley keeps to the plain sense: these are the ships of the sea by which riches were fetched from remote parts of the world.

Calvin weighs the trade itself before condemning it. Navigation cannot be condemned on its own account, since by importing and exporting merchandise it is of great advantage to mankind, and it is God’s will that the human race should be joined together by mutual acts of kindness; but abundance most frequently leads to pride, and in traffic with distant nations there is often much trickery and no limit set to the desire of gain. So the prophet describes covetousness by a sign, as one might express murder by holding out a bloody sword; and he adds the costly furniture because riches are usually the mother of superfluity, those who trade in distant countries not being satisfied with what is had at home but carrying away new luxuries formerly unknown—rich tapestry, and vessels framed with consummate skill. John Gill, continuing his application, reads the mountains and towers of the kingdoms and secular powers that support a later hierarchy, and the ships of its merchants. Keil and Delitzsch close by noting that the refrain returns with only a slight variation, the subjects of the two verbs transposed.
17:
The refrain returns, and the voices explain why. Charles Ellicott says the iteration is used as the most solemn form of emphasis, and that this was the burden of the prophet’s song. John Gill says the repetition serves for confirmation and certainty, and also to explain plainly what had before been said figuratively; he notes too that one interpreter refers the phrase that day here to the day of judgment. John Calvin makes the repetition settle the question the previous verses raised, since the prophet declares by it that he had his eye on men all along when he described the various kinds of loftiness: God is not displeased with the steep mountains or the tall cedars, which he created, and the whole evil lies in men who vainly trust in what is high. He then faces an objection squarely. It often happens that wicked men are not made humbler by chastisement but grow fiercer and more obstinate, as with the king whose hardness of heart no plagues could subdue, so that what is threatened here does not always come about. His answer is that the prophet is not describing the effect of chastisement, as though God bent rebellious men into obedience by it; the meaning is that although the hearts of the reprobate are not changed, the Lord will not cease to inflict punishment until their haughtiness and presumption are brought low—by chastisements so numerous and so severe that at length they are beaten down, cease to rise up against him, and acknowledge that they gain nothing by their insolence.

The verse on the idols is admired for its brevity. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the proclamation of judgment turns now to the no-gods, which, being at the root of all the evil, had occupied the lowest place in the list of things the land was full of; and that in a short verse of one clause consisting of only three words their future is declared as it were with a lightning-flash. The idols are one and all a mass of nothingness which will be reduced to absolute annihilation, and the word may mean either that they shall utterly perish or that they shall all perish—their images, their worship, and even their names and their memory. Ellicott makes the same observation from the other side: the seven words of the English answer to three in the Hebrew, and the prophet, with a profound sense of the power of rhythm, first condenses the judgment coming upon the no-gods and then expands it. He renders the clause accordingly, the no-gods shall pass away; Gill notes to the same effect that the word used signifies things that are not, since an idol is nothing in the world. Calvin points out the symmetry of the whole indictment, that as the prophet had joined idolatry with luxury and covetousness in his reproof, so he joins them again in the threatening of punishment. Adam Clarke adds that the ancient versions and a manuscript read the verb in the plural.
19:
The flight into the rocks is grounded in geography. Adam Clarke gathers the evidence: the country being mountainous and rocky is full of caverns, as appears from the history of David’s persecution, when one cave was so large that he and six hundred men hid in the sides of it while the king entered its mouth unaware. He adds reports of deep caves beyond Damascus one of which would hold four thousand men, and of a rocky mountain near Sidon in whose side two hundred chambers are hewn, each entered by an opening two feet square—places, he judges, contrived for the living and not the dead. Charles Ellicott keeps the earthquake of Uzziah’s reign still present to the prophet’s mind, and notes with Keil and Delitzsch the play on words in the last clause, which cannot be reproduced in English though the Latin gives some idea of it; they also distinguish the two nouns as a natural cave and a subterranean excavation. John Calvin marks a change of person: the prophet had earlier commanded them to enter the rock, to strike their minds the harder, whereas now he declares what they will do—so the former was no exhortation but a denunciation. The terror he identifies with what the Chaldeans and Assyrians brought, whose hand is called the Lord’s; and though those nations were wicked they promoted the glory of God, as even the devil contributes to it, contrary to his own wish. God is said to arise, Calvin adds, because he seems to sleep while he delays his judgments.

The casting away of the idols follows. Ellicott keeps the picture continuous: the men who have taken refuge in the caves fling away the idols they have found powerless, to the moles and bats which had their dwelling there—and it is perhaps significant that the creatures named were proverbial for blindness and love of darkness, fit custodians for gods whom none could worship but those that hated the light and were spiritually blind. Clarke says the same, that they carry their idols into the dark places to which they flee and there relinquish them to the animals in possession. Calvin uses the verse to strip away a defence: idolaters are delighted with their own superstitions, and though they abound in crimes they take refuge in the thought that their worship appeases God, so the prophet deprives them of this cloak, since the Lord will compel them to throw the idols away. In prosperity they suppose themselves in favour until God shows how greatly he abhors them—as another prophet illustrates by those who never acknowledge their wickedness while they make gain and live in splendour, but who, once stripped and forsaken, begin to think of their wretchedness. He presses the clause about the making too: what sort of gods can they be that were made by men, when God exists of himself and never had a beginning? Ellicott renders it more exactly, which they, the carvers, made for him, the worshipper. Keil and Delitzsch report that the traditional text divides the phrase about the moles into two words without its being possible to discover what they mean.

The last verse repeats the first with a difference, and Ellicott catches it. As men feel shock after shock, and see the flashing fires, and hear the crash of the thunder, they leave the larger caverns in which they first sought shelter—where they have left the idols that were once so precious—and fly to the smaller and higher openings in their unspeakable panic. John Gill notes that the words may mean either that the idolaters go there themselves or that they cast their idols there, and prefers the former; John Wesley identifies them as the idolatrous Israelites. Keil and Delitzsch close the strophe here, calling the whole a day of wrath appended to the earlier prophetic word.
22:
The closing verse is disputed both as to its text and as to where it belongs. Charles Ellicott reports that it is wanting in some manuscripts of the Greek version and has been rejected by some critics as being of the nature of a marginal comment and as not in harmony with the context. He weighs both objections and keeps the verse: the manuscript evidence is the more serious argument but is not decisive, while the second objection does not count for much, since to cease from man as well as from idols is surely the natural close of a discourse which had begun by proclaiming that men of all classes and conditions should be brought low. John Calvin takes the opposite view of its place, holding that the words are clearly connected with what follows and have been improperly separated from it—whoever made the division between the chapters, he says, has divided what ought to have been joined, since the opening of the next chapter explains and confirms exactly what is said here.

On the sense itself Calvin is firm against two other readings. Some refer the verse to Christ, taking the word for breath as a blast and the nostril as the seat of anger, so that the warning becomes one against provoking his wrath; but on a close examination of the words that is at variance with them. Others take it of men in general and explain it by the saying about not fearing those who can kill the body only; but that suits neither the time nor the occasion, since there was no call here to dissuade anyone from the fear of men. What the verse means, on his reading, is a rebuke of false confidence: I see that you are blinded and intoxicated by a groundless hope, so that no argument prevails with you, and this because you claim too much for yourselves—whereas man is nothing, and you have to do with God, who can reduce the whole world to nothing by a single act of his will. The breath in the nostrils denotes human weakness, the life of man being like a breath that immediately vanishes away, so that when the Lord takes it away man returns to his dust; and since nothing is more frail than our life, what can that confidence mean, as though our strength were deeply rooted?

The others say the same more briefly. Ellicott observes that the phrase about the breath emphasises the frailty of human life, and that it is on the ground of that frailty that the prophet asks, as the psalmist had asked, what such a creature is to be accounted of. John Wesley turns it into a rule—never admire or place your trust in man, whose breath is quickly stopped and taken away—and puts the closing question in the same form: what excellency is in him, considered in himself and without dependence upon God? Adam Clarke widens it by a step, that we are to trust neither in man nor in the gods he has invented, since neither he nor they can either save or destroy. John Gill, holding to the application he has followed through the chapter, reads it as advice to the followers of a claimant of divine honours to cease from going after him, seeing that he is not the living God but a dying man.
